schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'after these things' as a loose formula fixing nothing exactly (cf. Genesis 15:1; 22:1) and summarise Ezra's return with a royal commission; Ellicott reckons the gap at fifty-seven years, filled by the story of Esther, and 'son' by the genealogical law.
Clarke sets the seventh year about sixty-eight years after Cyrus and shows 'son of Seraiah' must mean descendant, else Ezra were 122; Wesley reads 'the son' as grandson.
Henry sees grace in Ezra's priesthood — God honouring a priesthood the captivity had eclipsed; takes Seraiah for the high priest slain at Riblah, not Ezra's immediate father.
Gill refers 'after these things' to the finished temple, its dedication, and the passover of the previous chapter.

debates.question: How large was the interval marked by 'after these things'?

sides.position: about sixty-eight years after Cyrus sent Zerubbabel back
fifty-seven years after the events just closed, spanning the story of Esther

schools.summary: Clarke: 'sopher machir' means not a swift penman but one skilled to expound the law (so the NT 'scribe,' the Syriac 'wise scribe'); Wesley reports the tradition that Ezra collected and fixed the Old Testament canon, a second Moses.

Ellicott hears the 'ready writer' of Psalms 45:1, sets the scribe's function as guarding and interpreting the law (v.10), and reads 'the hand of the LORD upon him' as the standing formula of special providence dear to Ezra and Nehemiah.
Henry makes the good hand of God the moral of the whole expedition — every creature is to us what God makes it, and we must see God's hand in events.
Gill notes this was Ezra's second going up from Babylon, distinct from the first return under Zerubbabel.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the partitive 'some' — a remnant of every order, laity and temple servants — and note the company's going with Ezra is stated in the edict (v.13) and the journey account (v.28).

Gill widens 'children of Israel' to include some of the ten tribes, and explains the long delay as caution: they waited to see Judea settle, then went up when the temple was finished and the returners prospered.
Henry reads the crowd that followed as the honour God put on Ezra — they would not stay in Babylon once he left, nor fear Jerusalem once he had gone thither.

Ellicott marks the doubled notes of time and the book's habit of summarising a company's arrival beforehand; Keil holds the framework — first of the first month to first of the fifth, all by the good hand of God.
Clarke reckons the journey at upwards of four months, slowed by the aged, infirm, women and children, and a circuitous route (cf. Ezra 8:24ff.).
Gill places the fifth month in high summer, answering to part of July and August.

Henry ties the good hand of God to both the king's favour and the safe journey, and reflects that God kept Ezra in Babylon until he had work for him — the book's own lesson of seeing God's hand in events.
Keil keeps the departure and arrival framework; Ellicott names 'the good hand of his God upon him' the full formula for the special providence Ezra and Nehemiah loved to own.
Gill names the first month Nisan (part of March and April) and its first day the Jewish New Year.
Clarke opens 'prepared' as fixed, purposed, determined with all his powers to seek, do, and teach the law; Wesley marks the observable order — understand for practice, then practise, then teach.

Ellicott traces the threefold movement of study, obedience, teaching as a perfect description of a congregation's teacher, and cautions that God's providence was the reason of Ezra's prepared heart, not its reward.
Henry: Ezra chose the law over Chaldean star-lore, and first learned then taught, first did then taught, so his example confirmed his doctrine.
Gill: Ezra set his heart to master the law by reading, searching, and meditating.

Ellicott makes the scribe's function weightier than the priest's — expositor of moral commandments and ceremonial statutes; Keil hears the Persian chancery terms for 'copy' and 'letter' (cf. Ezra 4:7, 11) and notes the Aramaic document begins.

Henry surveys the commission as ample beyond expectation, faults 'King of kings' as a title too high for a mortal, and notes Ezra prized 'scribe of the law of the God of heaven' above any court honour.
Wesley: 'the words of the commandments' is emphatic — Ezra explained both words and things to a people who had lost the language and the law.
Gill: 'the priest' is justly set first, Ezra being of high-priestly descent from Aaron.

Ellicott gives the Persian/Hebrew forms of Artaxerxes and traces 'king of kings' to Babylon (Daniel 2:37), noting the historian never uses the grand style; Keil reads the qualifier as 'the perfect scribe' (Vulgate 'doctissimo').
Gill defends 'king of kings' as truth not boast after Cyrus, citing Cyrus's tomb and Agamemnon at Troy.
Clarke marks the shift to Aramaic from here to v.26 and renders the royal name as the Persian 'Ardsheer shahinshah,' supreme king.
Clarke lingers on 'of their own freewill' — none forced to go or stay — and turns it into a probe: he who loves his God will seize the opportunity.
Gill reads 'I make a decree' as an unalterable law of the Medes and Persians — an irreversible charter, not a revocable favour.
Henry: the first article is leave to go up, since captives could not quit the realm without royal license.
Keil keeps the terms precise — laity and clergy alike, on the one condition of a willing mind, to travel in Ezra's charge.

themes: faith tested by an open door

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott identify the seven counsellors as the supreme court (Esther 1:14), Ellicott linking them to the families who aided Darius against the false Smerdis, and read the errand as an enquiry to conform Judah to the divine law.
Clarke finds the seven's names in Esther 1:10; Wesley reads the commission as inquiry into all abuses and their redress, the law being ever in Ezra's hand as his daily study.
Gill explains the Persian institution of seven counsellors from Darius Hystaspis, chosen out of seven nobles.

Henry's threefold reflection: the gift honours God among idolaters (cf. Psalms 45:12), praises a heathen king who honoured Israel's God, and reproaches the kings of Judah who plundered the temple a heathen now enriches.
Keil sorts the benefaction into three streams — crown, Gentile province, and countrymen — all flowing toward the one house at Jerusalem.
Gill takes it for a voluntary contribution of king and nobles for vessels or sacrifices, entrusted to Ezra.
Gill (with Jarchi) guards 'find' — no license to seize, but to take only what was freely offered, whatever Ezra could gather that way.
Wesley traces 'find' as 'procure' (cf. Genesis 6:8), a free gift not an exaction; Clarke: the king and counsellors had given, and Ezra may now receive whatever any inhabitant chose to add.
Ellicott reads the recurring 'which is in Jerusalem' as more than the period's fixed formula — a mark of deep reverence for the place God named.

Ellicott makes sacrifice the first priority, explains the meat- and drink-offerings by the rule of Numbers 15, and judges these liturgical phrases to be Ezra's own dictation into the decree; Keil reads the connecting particle as 'for this very reason.'
Gill marks the buying done 'with this money,' the sum freely contributed from every quarter.
Henry notes Ezra was trusted to lay out the money in the sacrifices offered on God's altar.

Ellicott weighs the clause of 'large latitude' as the means of beautifying the temple (v.27); Keil reads it as leaving all further disposal to Ezra and his brethren under the one condition of God's will.
Clarke marvels that the king bound them to no form or mode of worship, leaving everything to their own institutions.
Henry fixes on 'after the will of your God' as the king's own rule — let God's will govern what we lay out for his service.
Gill takes 'thy brethren' for the priests Ezra should call to his assistance.

Ellicott says the vessels were offered to be added to Zerubbabel's (cf. Ezra 8:25); Keil enlarges the donors to king, counsellors, princes, and all Israel, and glosses 'deliver' as to complete, consign, render up whole, 'before the God of Jerusalem.'
Gill distinguishes these new vessels of silver, gold, and fine copper from the old temple vessels Cyrus had already restored to Sheshbazzar.

themes: new gifts, not Cyrus's restored ones

schools.summary: Keil reads an open provision for unforeseen costs, drawn from the royal treasury via the treasurers beyond the river, and marks the emphatic 'I, even I'; Ellicott grounds it in each satrap's local treasury and foretells the qualification to come.
Henry admires the considerate warrant on the royal revenues — Ezra modest in demand, the king showing great affection for the temple and confidence in the man.
Gill takes the clause of further expenses for beautifying and adorning the temple.

themes: a draft on the royal treasury

schools.summary: Keil marks the emphatic royal self-assertion 'I, even I' and the swift obedience required of the treasurers, and (with Ellicott) notes the command runs straight into the schedule that caps the open draft of v.20.
Gill identifies the treasurers beyond the river as the receivers of royal tribute west of the Euphrates, toward the land of Israel.

Ellicott weighs the paradox — a restriction 'almost indefinite,' silver perhaps £24,000 — and grounds the grant in Palestine's produce, with salt unlimited because plentiful near the Dead Sea; Keil glosses the cor as the older chomer (1 Kings 5:2; Ezekiel 45:14).
Clarke gives the measures their content — the cor above seventy-five gallons, the bath some seven gallons — making the schedule a definite reckoning.
Gill values the hundred talents at some thirty-five thousand pounds, chiefly (per Jarchi) for the offerings.

Ellicott marks 'the God of heaven' twice and the king's deprecation of wrath, dates the seventh year to 458 B.C. amid Persia's reverses in Egypt, and notes the eighteen sons; Keil reads the verse as the ground of the whole authorisation.
Clarke enters the royal motive — Artaxerxes believed himself God's appointed and feared the kingdom cut off from his posterity if the work were neglected.
Gill grounds 'whatsoever is commanded by the God of heaven' in the law given by Moses.

themes: a heathen king's fear of wrath

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the emphatic 'we certify you' freeing the whole temple staff from every impost; Keil addresses it to the treasurers, forbidding toll, tribute, or custom on any servant of the house.
Gill notes the king's exact knowledge of the distinct offices — priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinim — so the exemption is granted with understanding.
Clarke supplies the fairness: men with no private revenue could not reasonably be taxed.
Henry draws the honour and its bound — dignity and freedom to serve, but only for need, not for trade and merchandise.

themes: a privilege tied to the calling

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott restrict 'all the people beyond the river' by 'such as know the laws of thy God' — Ezra made supreme over the Jewish population, with judges of their own nation, and charged both to judge and to teach.
Henry counts this the crowning favour — self-government under judges of Ezra's nomination, encouraged even to make proselytes by teaching the law.
Gill hears in 'the wisdom of thy God in thine hand' both Ezra's God-given wisdom and the law itself, framed with highest wisdom.
Wesley: the wisdom God put in Ezra's heart, shown in the works of his hand, to order the judicature of his people.

themes: wisdom and law in his hand

schools.summary: Keil identifies 'the law of the king' with the present edict and glosses banishment as a 'rooting out'; Ellicott stresses that civil authority is here added to religious, an unusual combination in one man demanding express statement.

Clarke: the penalties cover almost every species of punishment in a civilised state, and with this verse the Aramaic portion ends; Wesley wonders what David himself could have done more for God's honour.
Gill weighs two offenders — the judge who fails to execute justice, or the people who disobey God's law and the king's.

themes: the law of God and of the king
the end of the Aramaic letter

schools.summary: Henry marks the doxology in place of 'God save the king' — God put the thing into the king's heart, for he works in us to will and to do — and locates the temple's true beauty in ordinances rightly administered, not gilding.

Ellicott takes 'beautify' as the general restoration and the ejaculation as Ezra's own artless devotion (like Nehemiah's); Keil measures how Artaxerxes went beyond Cyrus and Darius in granting the community its own jurisdiction.
Gill: this is Ezra's thanksgiving to God for the whole decree.
Wesley: Ezra cannot proceed in his story without inserting this thankful acknowledgment of God's goodness.

themes: the true beautifying of the temple

schools.summary: Clarke admires the amiable piety that points past the king to the Lord God of the fathers as the true agent; Wesley draws the lesson — with God's hand we are bold, without it weak as water, and God must have all the glory.

Ellicott makes Ezra's ascription of court-honour to God's mercy the key to his humility; Keil notes the strengthened Ezra gathered the chief men of Israel to go up with him, as the next chapter records.
Henry sharpens the humility — the king eyed Ezra's merit, but Ezra, though a man of courage, ascribes preferment and strength wholly to God's mercy and hand.
Gill details the mercy: favour before king, counsellors, and nobles to carry the offerings, bear the commands, and lead up the willing Jews.

Keil lays out the priestly line to Aaron; Ellicott sets the omitted names under the genealogical law by which every ancestor is a 'father' and every descendant a 'son,' the links of 1 Chronicles 6 easily supplied.
Clarke counts sixteen generations here against twenty-two in 1 Chronicles 6:3ff., the gap to be filled between Meraioth (6:7) and Azariah son of Johanan (6:10).
Henry (with Wesley) notes the line carried up to Aaron with many names dropped for brevity, and reads the descent as God's fitting of a man for eminent service, as Moses in Egypt.
